14.0.0.en: Despair surrounded the Israelite people because of the strength of the Philistines and the small number of the army with Saul, but Jonathan was filled with hope and thought courageously of crossing the valley separating Michmash, where the Philistines were, from Gibeah of Benjamin. He asked the man who carried his weapons and accompanied him to go with him, and he deliberately did not tell his father, because he knew that he would prevent him from doing so.

14.1.0.en: As for Saul and the six hundred men with him, they hid and took shelter under the shade of a pomegranate tree to watch the Philistines from one edge of Gibeah. This pomegranate orchard was located in a region called Migron, which means “the slope.”

14.2.0.en: This verse is a parenthesis and has no bearing on the events, for it takes us to “Shiloh,” where the Tabernacle of Meeting is, and teaches us that the present priest, or the present high priest, who wears the ephod (one of the priestly garments), is “Ahiah,” whose uncle was “Ichabod” the son of Phinehas the son of Eli; and this Ichabod is the one whose mother died after bearing him (ch. 4:21). Perhaps Ahiah is Ahimelech, to whom David went in the city of Nob (ch. 22:9). Ahiah is mentioned here because King Saul will consult him in matters of war, as will come later (vv. 18, 19). After this we return to follow the events, and we learn that Jonathan went to the place of the Philistines without the knowledge of anyone of the people.

14.3.1.en: Seneh: a name given to the acacia tree.

14.3.2.en: To reach the Philistines, Jonathan had to cross a narrow pass in the valley, and on either side of this pass were two rocks facing each other, both sharp-pointed. The name of the first was Bozez and of the second Seneh; the top of the first rock was pointed toward the north in the direction of Michmash, and the other toward the south in the direction of Gibeah of Benjamin.

14.4.0.en: The uncircumcised: they are those who are not circumcised, and the Philistines are meant.

14.4.1.en: After the idea had matured in Jonathan’s mind, he opened to his armor-bearer what was in his heart to encourage him to go on with him, and he invited him to cross over to the camp of the Philistines, explaining the power of God, who is able to save at all times regardless of the number of the enemies.

14.5.0.en: The man’s answer was strong and spontaneous, and he said to Jonathan, do all that pleases you and that you see to be right, for I am with you and follow you in all that you do and in all that your heart and mind urge you to do.

14.5.1.en: The man’s answer to Jonathan carried more than one beautiful meaning; for despite the great danger, we find ourselves before a following, obedience, loyalty and manliness without equal. Would that we learn to obey the Church and our spiritual fathers, who will not expose us to dangers but protect us from them.

14.6.0.en: After Jonathan prayed, he spoke with his armor-bearer, saying, we will ask God to give us a sign, which is that we first show ourselves to the Philistines in a place midway between Gibeah and Michmash. If they say to us, “Stand still until we come to you,” we will know that God does not want us to go up to them, and we will return to Gibeah; but if the Philistines ask us to come up to them, we will know that God will give us strength and victory so that we go up and prevail over them.

14.7.0.en: Indeed the two crossed the narrow pass and showed themselves to the Philistines. The Philistines, with the utmost mockery and sarcasm, and in a figurative expression, described the two men as being like mice that come out of holes dug in the mountains; and of course what is meant is not Jonathan and his companion but all the Hebrews.

14.8.0.en: The men of the Philistines asked Jonathan and his servant to come up, and said to them, “Come up to us, and we will show you a thing,” the meaning being that they would defeat them so that they would know their weakness before the strength of the Philistines.

14.8.1.en: But Jonathan considered what the Philistines said to them about coming up to be the very sign awaited from God, and for this reason he encouraged his armor-bearer, saying that the Lord had delivered the Philistines into the hand of Israel, that is, that God would give us victory over them.

14.9.0.en: The hill on which the camp of the Philistines stood was steeply sloped, so Jonathan and his armor-bearer were compelled to go up on their hands and feet, climbing, and the Philistines were looking at them with scorn, since they were merely two going up to fight a great host of Philistines. This was an arrogance on the part of the Philistines which God allowed in order to make His power known to them with the humble, even if they were very few, that is, only two soldiers. So the Lord gave victory to Jonathan and his armor-bearer: Jonathan would kill those in front, and his armor-bearer would kill everyone who came from behind. To picture the situation, Jonathan and his armor-bearer placed their backs against each other so that each protected the other’s back.

14.10.0.en: Half a furrow of an acre: an expression and idiom meaning half the area that a plow plows in one day, which is a small area.

14.10.1.en: Jonathan and the man with him were able to kill twenty men of the Philistines in a very narrow area, in which the scouts of the Philistine camp were waiting; that is, they did not penetrate inward into Michmash, where the rest of the Philistine army was.

14.11.0.en: The host: the men drawn up in ranks and ready for war.

14.11.1.en: Fear and trembling fell on the hearts of the Philistines of every class, the scouts and those prepared in the camp, those in the fields, and the spoilers (highwaymen) among them. Perhaps they felt that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were the advance of large numbers of the children of Israel who had begun to attack them, in addition to the work of God, who cast fear into their hearts, so they fled in confusion and great fear.

14.12.0.en: As for the watchmen whom Saul had placed to watch the armies of the Philistines from the hill of Gibeah of Benjamin, they came down and told Saul all that they had seen, and how the Philistines were afraid and terrified with a great terror and fled and were scattered.

14.13.0.en: Saul naturally understood that someone had gone and done something that terrified the Philistines, so he ordered a counting and numbering of his men. Indeed the numbering was done, and it resulted in the discovery of the absence of Jonathan and the man who was his armor-bearer.

14.14.0.en: Ahiah was the high priest at that time, and the Ark had been moved from “Kirjath-jearim” to Gibeah of Benjamin, where the camp of Saul and his men was. So Saul asked the priest Ahiah to stand before the Ark to ask the Lord what Israel should do.

14.15.0.en: Ahiah indeed began to pray and sought God’s counsel, but with the confusion of the Philistines and the increase of their shouting as they withdrew, Saul was relatively reassured. And, again in an unjustified haste, he ordered the priest to stop praying and lifting his hands to God. This shows his pride and his lack of concern to submit to the voice of God.

14.16.0.en: Saul raised the battle cry, thereby driving all the people with him to war and to set out toward the place of the Philistines, who in their fear hurried to come out of the pass of Michmash; and in their crowding, each of them began to kill the one near him so that safety would be written for him alone ... so they were killing one another.

14.17.0.en: As for the Hebrews who had been occupied by the Philistines at Michmash or around it, they joined Saul, who with his son Jonathan drew near to them, and they fought with them the rest of the Philistines. So did all the Israelites hiding from the Philistines in the caves of Mount Ephraim when they heard of the defeat of the Philistines; all were strengthened and pursued the fleeing Philistines.

14.18.0.en: Beth-aven: the house of idols, located between Bethel and Michmash.

14.18.1.en: The Lord gave deliverance to His people by means of a small number of men, and after the battle had been at Michmash in the lands of the Israelites, it moved to a place called Beth-aven west of Michmash.

14.18.2.en: God is the maker of victory, and it is for you to follow through and complete your victory over Satan. When God lifts some sin from you, your holding fast to His commandments must increase and you must complete your spiritual striving, so that Satan fears and flees from you.

14.19.0.en: Distressed: distress and bitterness of soul.

14.19.1.en: Before this victory, Saul did not want to give the Philistines any opportunity to reorganize their ranks, and for this reason he swore before God and his men that none of them should taste food or drink until the end of the day, so that they might complete their victory in their pursuit. Before this oath none of the men could break it, but distress, exhaustion and hidden murmuring came upon them. Of course this was not a wise action on the part of Saul, who did not take into account his men’s need for rest and food to sustain them.

14.19.2.en: Several mistakes into which Saul fell by this decision appear from this:

14.19.3.en: 1- He did not care to hear the voice of God from the mouth of Ahiah (v. 19).

14.19.4.en: 2- He neglected his men’s need for food and burdened them with fasting, so that they almost collapsed from hunger during the battle.

14.19.5.en: 3- The men’s severe hunger led them to fall into an error, for they slaughtered on the blood and ate, although God forbade the eating of blood, as will appear in the following verses.

14.19.6.en: 4- He regarded the Philistines as his enemies, when he should have said the enemies of God, for it is by the power of God that he prevails over them and not by his own power (v. 24).

14.20.0.en: The forest: an area of trees in the midst of a valley, and it also comes in the sense of a difficult road.

14.20.1.en: Saul and his men advanced into an area where trees were abundant, and bees had made hives for themselves in these trees and filled them with honey until it overflowed and fell from the trees and covered the whole ground of the area in its abundance. Yet the people, despite their weariness and exhaustion, did not dare to put forth their hand and eat of this honey, for fear of their oath before God and before Saul.

14.21.0.en: The end of the rod: a staff.

14.21.1.en: His eyes were enlightened: his strength returned to him.

14.21.2.en: Jonathan was not present when his father Saul bound the people with the previous oath, and for this reason, when he and his armor-bearer caught up with the people at the forest, he stretched out his staff to the fallen honey of the bees and ate of it and regained his strength and vigor. One of the people saw him eating of the honey and told him that his father had bound the people with an oath and with the falling of a curse on the man who eats before the end of the battle, which had exhausted the people, distressed them and wearied them greatly.

14.22.0.en: Jonathan did not flatter his father but said sincerely, “My father has erred by this oath and caused distress to everyone.” He gave himself as an example, that when he ate of the honey he regained his health, so how had his father made this error, for if the men of the children of Israel had eaten of this honey they would have regained their strength and been able to finish off the rest of the Philistines.

14.23.0.en: Aijalon: the last city in the tribe of Dan, located on the border of the Philistines.

14.23.1.en: Saul’s men followed the Philistines and pursued them a long distance from Michmash to “Beth-aven,” and from “Beth-aven” to “the forest,” and from the forest to “Aijalon,” which is the last city on the border between the lands of the Hebrews in the tribe of Gad and the lands of the Philistines; but the people had reached the utmost degree of weariness and exhaustion.

14.23.2.en: Saul rushed in and swore and made a covenant that no one should taste food until the battle was finished, and by this he wearied his soldiers. So be wise and seek God’s counsel before you rush into any commitment or vow, and if time permits you, seek the counsel of your spiritual father.

14.24.s.en: (4) Eating the sacrifices with their blood

14.24.0.en: No sooner had the battle ended than the hungry people turned to the spoil of the Philistines, the animals, and took some for themselves and slaughtered and ate on the very ground on which the animals’ blood was shed, which is contrary to the Law (Lev 17:10-16). In their haste and hurry they did not wait until the animals had drained all their blood, and they did not slaughter them on a high place that would allow the blood to drain downward, so their eating was mixed with the blood of the animals, which is considered contrary to the Law.

14.25.0.en: Out of fear of God’s wrath and punishment, some of the men went to Saul and told him of the people’s error when they ate the sacrifices with their blood. Saul answered that what the men had done was treachery against the Lord, and he asked the men to roll a great stone to make an altar of it.

14.26.0.en: Saul commanded his officers to spread out among the people and tell them that whoever wants to slaughter and eat of his spoil should bring what he wants to slaughter to this high stone (the altar) and then eat what is pleasing to them, without sinning against God or angering Him. The people responded to Saul’s word, and all of them slaughtered on this stone.

14.27.0.en: In acknowledgment of the work of God, Saul built another altar to the Lord on which to offer burnt offerings and thank offerings, and this was of course through the priest “Ahiah.” The expression “he began to build an altar to the Lord” distinguishes it from the first stone, which he made for slaughtering the spoils of war for the people. Saul had begun to build it and did not finish it, and this is the first altar that Saul built to the Lord.

14.28.0.en: Saul wanted to exploit the victory to the end and take the spoil of the Philistines, so he met with the leaders of his people and proposed that they continue the battle by night and attack the lands of the Philistines until the morning of the next day in order to destroy them and take the rest of their spoil. Because the people had eaten and rested, Saul agreed to their proposal that he do what he saw to be right, but “Ahiah the priest proposed that they stand before God to know His will before beginning to do anything.

14.29.0.en: Saul asked the Lord, by means of the high priest, about his proposal and whether God would stand with His people and deliver the Philistines to them, but God did not answer him anything, that is, He did not say yes or no. Of course Saul did not continue the battle, since the Lord did not give him approval.

14.29.1.en: Note: Inquiring of the Lord by means of the high priest was done through two precious stones, the “Urim” and the “Thummim,” on one of which was written yes and on the other no. If the first stone was lit up, the answer was God’s consent, and if the other was lit up, the answer was God’s refusal, but if neither lit up, this meant that God gave His people no reply.

14.29.2.en: In the exhilaration of joy and the need of hunger, the people ate the sacrifices with their blood ... So it is good for a person in his joy not to break God’s commandments by stumbling behaviors such as dancing, drinking wine or wearing improper clothing ...

14.30.0.en: It was strange that God did not answer His people with yes or no, and for this reason Saul concluded that God was angry with them and that one of the men of the people had committed a great sin that was the cause of this, and this is what made Saul speak to his people about it.

14.31.0.en: In a new haste on Saul’s part, he swore by the living Lord, the Savior of Israel, that if the guilty person who was the cause of God’s not answering were found, he would put him to death, whoever he might be, even if it were Jonathan his son. As for the people who were listening to Saul, they did not answer him, and no one uttered a single word ... because they knew that the cause was Jonathan, but he was beloved by all.

14.32.0.en: Saul decided to cast lots to find the guilty one, and so as not to exempt himself or Jonathan his son, he decided to cast the lot in more than one stage. The first stage would be between himself and his son on one side and all the people on the other; if he and his son were cleared, he would then cast the lot on the tribes and then the clans until he reached the sinner, which was the system followed at that time. As for the people’s answer, it was submission to what their king proposed to them.

14.33.0.en: Give a perfect lot: show us the truth and declare what is true.

14.33.1.en: Before casting the first lot, Saul addressed God in a quick prayer, saying, “Lord, declare the truth, and let this lot be according to Your will to reveal the person who has erred.” When the lot was cast, the people came out of it innocent, and Saul and his son Jonathan remained. Then Saul asked for the lot to be cast a second time to determine the person; Saul was cleared, and the lot took his son Jonathan.

14.34.0.en: Saul was surprised by the result of the lot, which was something he had basically ruled out, and for this reason he asked Jonathan for an explanation of the error he had committed. Jonathan answered him with what had happened, that he had eaten a little honey (although he did so without knowing his father’s prohibition), and he went on to say that since the lot had taken him, he was ready to die, because it was the will of God. By this Jonathan accepted death without any fault of his, because he did not know his father’s oath, and in this he is a symbol of Christ, who died on the Cross without sinning in order to redeem His people. Jonathan gave victory to his people and accepted to die for them, and Christ gave the victory over Satan by the Cross, by His death for His people.

14.34.1.en: Notice with me, beloved, how Jonathan did not defend himself by saying that he did not know of his father’s command or that his father’s command was wrong in the first place, but in wonderful submission offered himself to death, believing that the lot that fell on him was a divine ordering and therefore he must respond ...!!! Defend yourself gently and leave the matter in God’s hand, and when you do so you will find God glorified, sending one to defend you and revealing the truth, as we shall see now in what happened.

14.35.0.en: Saul did not draw back but issued the sentence of death on his son Jonathan, using the expression “God do so and more also,” which is an expression meaning that God would do something harsher than death if he did not carry out the sentence of death on his son.

14.36.0.en: The people defended Jonathan with a strong and moving defense, since on the one hand they loved him, and on the other hand Jonathan was the cause of the defeat of the Philistines and the deliverance of Israel, and this would not have happened had it not been for God’s support of him. The people swore in the face of Saul that no harm should befall Jonathan, not even the falling of a single hair of his head. The expression “the people rescued Jonathan” means that by their strong and vigorous defense they saved him from death. Most likely Saul offered sacrifices for his haste in the oath, and Jonathan also offered sacrifices for his unintentional error.

14.37.0.en: Since Saul received no answer from God to continue the battle, he and his men withdrew, and so the Philistines went each to his own town. But the wars with the Philistines continued, as appears in the following verses and in (ch. 31), in which Saul will die.

14.38.0.en: The Philistines: they dwelt on the southern border of the land of Israel.

14.38.1.en: Moab and the children of Ammon: descendants of Lot, who dwelt east of the Jordan River and the Dead Sea.

14.38.2.en: Edom: descendants of Esau, who dwelt on the southern border of the children of Israel in the mountains of Seir.

14.38.3.en: Zobah: a city of the Arameans.

14.38.4.en: The kingdom was fully established and settled for Saul over Israel, and he had no opponent. Saul took advantage of the people’s rallying around him and waged a group of small wars on his enemies surrounding the borders of the land of the children of Israel, and the Lord gave him victory over the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Edomites and the Philistines, who are all the pagan peoples on the borders of Israel. In all his wars Saul was fierce and strong, so he was also able to smite the mighty Amalekites, who anciently dwelt in Sinai and, in his days, in the south of Palestine, and he prevented all the plunderers and spoilers from attacking the lands of the tribes.

14.39.0.en: These three verses are an introduction to Saul’s family and his small and large household ... The introduction began first with his male children: Jonathan his firstborn, and the second, Ishui, who is also called “Abinadab” (ch. 31:2), and his third son, “Melchishua”; there was also a fourth son called “Ishbosheth” (2 Sam 2:8). His two daughters were “Merab” and “Michal,” whom David later married. Saul’s lawful wife was “Ahinoam,” and he had another concubine, “Rizpah.” His uncle was “Ner” and his cousin “Abner,” to whom he entrusted the command of the army; as for Saul’s grandfather, his name was “Abiel,” and he was also called by another name, “Ner” (1 Chr 9:39), which is the name his son, that is, Saul’s uncle, also bore.

14.40.0.en: At the close of the chapter, the inspired text tells us that all the days of Saul’s reign over Israel there were wars with the Philistines, and it also mentions that Saul was a good commander, for he would attach every strong and mighty man to his army, which showed the strength of Israel.

14.40.1.en: It was a beautiful quality in Saul that he attached every strong man to his army, so you should hold fast to everything that strengthens you in your spiritual warfare against Satan, such as the Holy Bible, repentance, Holy Communion, prayer and every opportunity for spiritual meetings ...

14.40.2.en: The victory over the Amalekites and God’s rejection of Saul
